goal: build a Hack assembler in C

nodes.description: Separate program instructions from comments and blank lines.

nodes.title: Binary representation
nodes.description: Understand how numbers become fixed-width sequences of bits.

nodes.title: Hack instructions
nodes.description: Recognize the address and computation forms of the Hack language.

nodes.title: C strings & arrays
nodes.description: Work with character buffers, string boundaries, and simple comparisons.

nodes.title: File input & output
nodes.description: Read a source file and write a clean output file.

nodes.title: Instruction encoding
nodes.description: Translate valid instructions into the bits defined by the Hack specification.

nodes.title: Symbol tables
nodes.description: Associate names with addresses using a simple table.

nodes.description: Resolve labels first, then translate instructions and allocate variables.

nodes.title: Hack assembler
nodes.description: Build a command-line assembler that translates Hack assembly into matching .hack output. Validate it against the official reference tool.

resources.title: GNU C Language Introduction and Reference Manual

tasks.title: Make your first C program run
tasks.exercise: Write a small C program that stores the integers 2 and 3, adds them, and prints the result. Compile it with a C compiler and run it yourself.
tasks.expectedOutput: Your program compiles successfully and prints 5 when you run it. Keep the source file and a note of the command you used.
tasks.explanation: Your assembler will be written in C. Getting a small program to compile and run gives you a starting point before handling text input. Python and JavaScript experience helps, but does not establish familiarity with C.

tasks.title: Find the instructions in the noise
tasks.exercise: Create a small Hack assembly input containing @2, D=A, and @3 on separate lines. Add blank lines, full-line comments, and an inline comment. Write a C program that reads the input and emits only the instructions, in their original order.
tasks.expectedOutput: An ordered list containing @2, D=A, and @3. Blank lines and comments are excluded, including the comment after an instruction.
tasks.explanation: You marked C essentials as prior knowledge, so the introductory C task is skipped. An assembler needs to identify instructions before translating them. Practise that small step before tackling the complete project.

tasks.title: Put numbers into bits
tasks.exercise: Convert 0, 2, and 32767 to sixteen-bit binary representations. Explain which part of an address instruction holds its numeric value.
tasks.expectedOutput: Three fixed-width binary representations and a short explanation of an address instruction.
tasks.explanation: Encoding requires understanding fixed-width bits before translating the Hack language.

tasks.title: Recognize the two instruction forms
tasks.exercise: Read the official Hack language reference. Classify a small set of address and computation instructions and identify their fields.
tasks.expectedOutput: A labelled set of examples distinguishing addresses from computation, destination, and jump fields.
tasks.explanation: You need to identify each instruction form before assigning its binary fields.

tasks.title: Handle text without losing its boundaries
tasks.exercise: Create a character buffer, find its terminating null, and compare two short strings. Explain what happens when the input is too long for the buffer.
tasks.expectedOutput: A small program and notes demonstrating string length, comparison, and a safe length limit.
tasks.explanation: Strings and arrays help represent names safely. They support text parsing but are not an extra blocker for the first parsing exercise.

tasks.title: Read a file, write a result
tasks.exercise: Read a small text file one line at a time and write its nonempty lines to a new file. Handle missing files and close opened streams.
tasks.expectedOutput: An input file, an output file, and a clear failure message when the input cannot be opened.
tasks.explanation: The final assembler takes an .asm file and produces a .hack file. File handling makes that workflow repeatable.

tasks.title: Translate instructions into bits
tasks.exercise: Using the official Hack specification, implement numeric address translation and lookup tables for computation, destination, and jump fields. Start without symbols.
tasks.expectedOutput: Tests showing sixteen output bits for each valid instruction, matched against the reference assembler.
tasks.explanation: This is the first working translation stage. Numeric instructions can be tested before symbol handling is added.

tasks.title: Give names an address
tasks.exercise: Use a simple array of name/address records. Add a name, look it up, and handle a missing name. Start with a fixed-size table rather than a new data-structure course.
tasks.expectedOutput: A small table implementation with lookup, insertion, and boundary tests.
tasks.explanation: A modest symbol table is enough for this project. It connects readable labels and variable names to numeric addresses.

tasks.title: Resolve names before translating
tasks.exercise: Extend your translator with a first pass that records label addresses and a second pass that resolves variables and emits instructions. Follow the official symbol rules.
tasks.expectedOutput: Symbolic test inputs produce the same output as the reference assembler, including forward label references.
tasks.explanation: Labels may be used before their definitions. Two passes let the assembler resolve them consistently.

tasks.title: Make invalid input understandable
tasks.exercise: Add checks for malformed instructions and file failures. Report a clear reason and the original source line instead of producing misleading output.
tasks.expectedOutput: Invalid-input cases produce useful messages and a failure exit status.
tasks.explanation: Good error messages make the assembler easier to debug and prevent invalid output from looking successful.

tasks.title: Compare with a trusted reference
tasks.exercise: Use the official Project 6 test programs. Compare your generated files with output from the reference assembler and record differences. Include numeric and symbolic inputs.
tasks.expectedOutput: A repeatable comparison procedure with results for the supplied test programs.
tasks.explanation: Matching a reference provides practical evidence of correct translation; merely reading a resource does not.

tasks.title: Connect the complete command
tasks.exercise: Join file input, parsing, encoding, symbol handling, and validation behind one command that accepts an .asm path and writes a .hack file.
tasks.expectedOutput: A reproducible command, output file, and short usage instructions for another person.
tasks.explanation: Integration brings the separate learning steps together into a useful project.

tasks.title: Demonstrate your assembler
tasks.exercise: Run the integrated assembler against the official Project 6 programs. Compare output with the reference tool and explain your two-pass design from your own implementation.
tasks.expectedOutput: Matching outputs, a repeatable validation record, and an explanation of how your assembler works.
tasks.explanation: This is the project destination. Validation is performed by you; the learning planner does not execute or grade your program.
